segments.text: This chapter builds the classical theory of electric and magnetic fields, culminating in Maxwell’s equations — four equations that unify electricity, magnetism, and light into a single framework. Its logical order moves from static charges (electrostatics) to static currents (magnetostatics) to the coupling between changing fields (electromagnetic induction), and finally to the complete, time-dependent theory.

Its power is computational: for situations with high symmetry (a sphere, an infinite line, or an infinite plane of charge), Gauss’s law lets you find the field with simple algebra instead of a difficult direct integration over every charge element.

Materials respond to an applied magnetic field in three broad categories, depending on their atomic magnetic moments:
materials are weakly repelled (induced moments oppose the field);
materials are weakly attracted (existing atomic moments partially align with the field but are randomised by thermal motion);

materials (iron, cobalt, nickel) show strong, persistent magnetisation because neighbouring atomic moments align cooperatively within regions called domains, which is why they can form permanent magnets.

blocks.text: 6. Faraday’s law of induction and AC circuits

segments.text: , EMF = −dΦ_B/dt, states that a changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an electromotive force (voltage) — the basis of electric generators, transformers, and inductors. The negative sign is
: the induced current always opposes the change that caused it, consistent with energy conservation.

blocks.text: 7. Maxwell’s equations, the Poynting vector, and potentials

segments.text: summarise all of classical electromagnetism: Gauss’s law for E, Gauss’s law for B (stating magnetic monopoles do not exist — field lines always close on themselves), Faraday’s law, and the Ampère–Maxwell law (Ampère’s law extended with Maxwell’s crucial addition of a “displacement current” term, needed for consistency and which predicts that a changing electric field itself generates a magnetic field). Together, these equations show that a self-sustaining electromagnetic wave can propagate through empty space at speed c — unifying electricity, magnetism, and optics.

items.text: Gauss’s law and Ampère’s law exploit symmetry to compute fields easily; potential (a scalar) is often more convenient than field (a vector) and obeys Poisson’s/Laplace’s equations.

Dielectrics increase capacitance by polarizing and partially cancelling the applied field; magnetic materials are classified by how their atomic moments respond (diamagnetic, paramagnetic, ferromagnetic).
Faraday’s law (changing flux induces EMF) and Lenz’s law (the induced effect opposes the change) underlie generators, transformers, and AC circuit behaviour, including resonance.
Maxwell’s equations unify electricity and magnetism and predict electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light; the Poynting vector describes the energy such waves carry.
